prompt: Some cities have made all public transport free to use, paying for it through taxation instead of fares. Do you think this is a positive or negative development?
essay:
Abolishing fares is one of the few transport policies that are popular before they are introduced and remain popular afterwards, and that is part of the difficulty. It tends to be judged by who travels free rather than by what the money could otherwise have bought. Judged the second way, I think free public transport is a negative development in most of the cities that have considered it, though an understandable one.

The case for it deserves to be stated fairly. Fares are regressive: a monthly pass is a trivial sum to a lawyer and a serious one to a cleaner, and for people on low incomes the price of travel can determine which jobs are within reach at all. Free travel also removes the cost of printing, selling and inspecting tickets, and in a small city where fares raise relatively little, that saving can go a long way towards paying for the policy.

The trouble is that price is seldom what keeps people off public transport. What keeps them in their cars is time, reliability and the absence of a service at the hours they need one; a free bus that comes every forty minutes is still a bus that comes every forty minutes. Removing fares therefore mostly rewards people who were already travelling, while the fare revenue that might have paid for more frequent services has gone. A city that makes transport free without enlarging its budget has, in effect, chosen a cheaper ticket over a better network, and those who depend on the network most are the ones who lose.

The social aim is right, but it can be met more precisely. Free or heavily discounted travel for people on low incomes, for students and for the elderly delivers most of the fairness at a fraction of the cost, and leaves the fares paid by everyone else to fund frequency and reach. Only where a city can afford both free travel and more services does the blanket policy make sense. Elsewhere it is a generous gesture paid for out of the quality of the very service it was meant to improve.
title: Making public transport free
